title: Customer validation: find ten people who say they'll buy before you build
summary: Jason argues that the minimum proof for a startup idea is ten real people saying they'll pay. He dismantles the common excuses (scratching your own itch, mock-ups don't work, a great product sells itself, friends like it) and says to attack the riskiest non-code parts of the business first.

principles.text: Before building, find ten people who say they'll buy it; otherwise the company isn't real.
principles.quote: If you can't find ten people who say they'll buy it, your company is bullshit.

principles.text: Being your own customer is only the spark of an idea, not market validation.
principles.quote: "Scratching your own itch" is how all three of my companies started, but it's only that--the start.

principles.text: If the market is millions strong, finding ten buyers is trivial; failing means the market isn't there or isn't interested.
principles.quote: If there are millions, it's trivial to find ten. If you can't find even ten, then either there's not millions or those millions aren't interested in you.

principles.text: You should be able to validate with a short pitch or mock-up; a 30-second pitch is the test of a clear concept.
principles.quote: If your concept is so esoteric that you can't describe it in 30 seconds at a cocktail party, it's either too complex or you don't understand it yourself.

principles.text: Good software alone doesn't make a business, so tackle the riskiest non-code unknowns (finding and convincing customers) first.
principles.quote: If your goal is a business (not a hobby), building charming, novel software isn't enough.

principles.text: Only willingness to pay counts as validation, not opinions from friends, family or even experts.
principles.quote: The only thing that matters is that people are willing to give you money!
